stem: A 74-year-old with LVEF 25% presents with orthopnoea, bilateral crackles, JVP elevation and pitting oedema. BP is 158/92 mmHg, HR 94/min, SpO2 91% on room air. He is alert with warm extremities and no chest pain.

stem: A 29-year-old following a high-speed collision has GCS 7, unilateral dilated pupil, BP 176/84 mmHg and HR 48/min. SpO2 is 93% on oxygen. No major external haemorrhage is evident.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate immediate management?

stem: A 29-year-old at 40 weeks is receiving oxytocin augmentation. CTG shows baseline 175/min, minimal variability and recurrent late decelerations. There are seven uterine contractions per ten minutes. BP is 114/70 mmHg and labour is not close to vaginal delivery.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Give maternal oxygen and IV fluids without altering the oxytocin infusion.
Stop oxytocin, correct reversible causes and escalate the abnormal CTG.
Reduce oxytocin slightly and reassess the CTG over 30 minutes.
Continue infusion while arranging fetal scalp stimulation and a repeat CTG.
Provide maternal repositioning and await spontaneous CTG recovery for one hour.
explanations: Oxygen alone cannot reverse excessive contraction frequency or eliminate need for escalation. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Stop oxytocin, reposition mother, correct reversible causes and urgently involve senior obstetrics for possible expedited delivery. stem: A 60-year-old with untreated Streptococcus aureus bacteraemia develops sudden severe dyspnoea and pulmonary oedema. A new early diastolic murmur is heard and echocardiography shows flail aortic cusp with severe regurgitation and vegetation. BP is 86/46 mmHg.
ask: Which treatment plan is MOST appropriate?
options: Arrange urgent transoesophageal imaging before contacting the surgical team.

explanations: A further transoesophageal study may be useful for operative planning, but echo already shows destructive acute aortic regurgitation with shock. Emergency surgery consultation and haemodynamic support should proceed without waiting for repeat imaging.

Pain plus fetal collapse and loss of station is not normal scar stretching. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Stop oxytocin, activate an emergency obstetric response, resuscitate and proceed urgently to laparotomy/birth. New pain, fetal bradycardia and loss of presenting-part station during VBAC are classic rupture red flags.
pearl: New pain, fetal bradycardia and loss of presenting-part station during VBAC are classic rupture red flags.
pivot: With an intact uterus but uncomplicated uterine tachysystole and reassuring fetus, oxytocin reduction and conservative measures may suffice.

steps: Stop oxytocin, call consultant obstetrics/anaesthetics/neonatal and activate massive haemorrhage support.
ABCDE, large-bore access, bloods/crossmatch, blood products, oxygen if hypoxaemic, maternal left tilt.
Emergency laparotomy and delivery; repair versus hysterectomy depending extent and haemostasis.
Post-haemorrhage/ICU monitoring, counselling about future pregnancy risks.
management.safety: Do not delay surgery for confirmatory ultrasound if clinical rupture and fetal compromise are clear.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

skill: Necrotising soft tissue infection / source control
stem: A 55-year-old with diabetes has rapidly progressive leg pain two days after a small cut. Pain is far worse than surface erythema; there is purple mottling, bullae, fever 39.2 °C, BP 86/48 mmHg and lactate 5.0. Crepitus is absent.
ask: Which is the BEST management?
options: Give IV corticosteroids and antibiotics for presumed severe inflammatory cellulitis.
Order MRI first to delineate fascial involvement before surgical intervention.
Give antibiotics and urgently debride suspected necrotising fasciitis.
Perform bedside incision and drainage with local anaesthetic, then observe.
Give IV flucloxacillin and await development of definite crepitus.
explanations: Steroids are not definitive treatment and may worsen infection without source control. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Start resuscitation, urgent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and immediate surgical exploration/debridement. Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and rapidly evolving skin signs are early necrotising fasciitis clues even without gas.

MRI can be helpful in uncertain stable cases but should not delay antibiotics or exploration in shock. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Start resuscitation, urgent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and immediate surgical exploration/debridement. Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and rapidly evolving skin signs are early necrotising fasciitis clues even without gas.

Correct: necrotising fasciitis is a surgical source-control emergency; imaging should not delay surgery when suspicion is high. Clinical distinction: Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and rapidly evolving skin signs are early necrotising fasciitis clues even without gas.

Absence of crepitus does not exclude necrotising infection; delay allows rapid progression. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Start resuscitation, urgent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and immediate surgical exploration/debridement. Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and rapidly evolving skin signs are early necrotising fasciitis clues even without gas.

Shock and pain out of proportion indicate potential necrotising infection; outpatient antibiotics are unsafe. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Start resuscitation, urgent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and immediate surgical exploration/debridement. Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and rapidly evolving skin signs are early necrotising fasciitis clues even without gas.
pearl: Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and rapidly evolving skin signs are early necrotising fasciitis clues even without gas.
pivot: Uncomplicated cellulitis without systemic toxicity or deep pain can be treated with appropriate antibiotics and follow-up.

steps: Sepsis resuscitation, call general/orthopaedic/plastic surgery plus ICU immediately.
Broad IV coverage for Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria, with antitoxin agent where toxin-mediated streptococcal infection suspected.
Urgent extensive debridement and repeat theatre assessments; imaging only if it does not delay source control.
Lactate, renal function, shock support, wound cultures and antibiotic tailoring.
management.safety: Do not wait for crepitus, high LRINEC score or normal skin to declare the process safe.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 24-year-old has slept under two hours nightly for nine days, is excessively talkative, has spent her savings on a 'global media company' and believes her television is communicating directly with her. She is agitated and refuses food. No illicit substances detected.
ask: Which immediate management is MOST appropriate?
options: Start intensive psychological treatment while withholding mood stabilisation.
Plan rapid community review because no self-harm thoughts were reported.
Begin antidepressant treatment and reassess sleep at the next appointment.
Admit for urgent risk assessment and antimanic treatment.
Diagnose hypomania and offer short-term sedative medication at home.
explanations: Psychotherapy can assist with engagement and relapse prevention, but acute mania with delusions, severe sleep loss and refusal of food generally requires prompt medical and psychiatric care.
Mania does not require depressive symptoms. Psychosis, dangerous impulsivity and marked impairment make this presentation severe and not suitable for routine discharge.
Antidepressant monotherapy may precipitate or worsen mania and does not adequately treat agitation and delusional beliefs. Treat the mood episode with specialist-guided antimanic strategies.

Correct: this is a manic episode with psychotic symptoms and impaired self-care. Perform urgent risk and capacity assessment, obtain a safe environment, arrange acute psychiatric admission as indicated and initiate appropriate antipsychotic and mood stabilising treatment while assessing medical and substance-related causes.
Hypomania does not involve psychosis or marked functional impairment. Articulate speech does not diminish the significance of delusions, self-neglect or hazardous spending.
pearl: Mania is a mood episode with marked impairment or psychosis; psychotic features automatically exclude hypomania.
pivot: A shorter elevated mood period without marked impairment or psychosis may represent hypomania, affecting the bipolar subtype.

steps: Risk to self/others, food/fluid intake, sleep deprivation, finances, substance use, medical causes and decision capacity.
Low-stimulation supervised setting; short-term antipsychotic with adjunct benzodiazepine as needed and mood stabiliser strategy under psychiatry.
ECG, metabolic profile, pregnancy status and medication risks; restore nutrition/hydration and sleep.
Psychoeducation, early relapse signals, adherence and family engagement with consent.
management.safety: Lithium, valproate and antipsychotic selection require pregnancy/reproductive counselling and monitoring.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A patient is being treated for a large amitriptyline ingestion. After initial sodium bicarbonate, BP improves but ECG again shows QRS 160 ms with recurrent ventricular ectopics. Arterial pH is 7.43, potassium 3.7 mmol/L.
ask: What should the team prioritise?
options: Use atropine to treat persistent conduction toxicity and ventricular ectopy.
Administer flecainide for rhythm stabilisation alongside intensive monitoring.
Repeat IV sodium bicarbonate under ECG and pH monitoring.
Administer another dose of activated charcoal to limit toxin absorption.
Give physostigmine to reverse the toxic antimuscarinic syndrome.
explanations: Atropine is for symptomatic bradycardia, not TCA tachyarrhythmia. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Repeat sodium bicarbonate under ECG and acid-base monitoring with toxicology support. Treat TCA cardiotoxicity by QRS and haemodynamics, not solely mental state or serum concentration.

Class Ic agents intensify sodium-channel blockade and are unsafe in TCA poisoning. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Repeat sodium bicarbonate under ECG and acid-base monitoring with toxicology support. Treat TCA cardiotoxicity by QRS and haemodynamics, not solely mental state or serum concentration.

Correct: recurrent QRS widening implies ongoing sodium-channel toxicity and often needs additional bicarbonate. Clinical distinction: Treat TCA cardiotoxicity by QRS and haemodynamics, not solely mental state or serum concentration.

Airway/cardiac stabilisation is priority and oral charcoal risks aspiration. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Repeat sodium bicarbonate under ECG and acid-base monitoring with toxicology support. Treat TCA cardiotoxicity by QRS and haemodynamics, not solely mental state or serum concentration.

Physostigmine is contraindicated with significant conduction delay and seizure risk. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Repeat sodium bicarbonate under ECG and acid-base monitoring with toxicology support. Treat TCA cardiotoxicity by QRS and haemodynamics, not solely mental state or serum concentration.
pearl: Treat TCA cardiotoxicity by QRS and haemodynamics, not solely mental state or serum concentration.
pivot: Once ECG and haemodynamics remain stable and toxicity resolves, observation and psychiatry assessment guide disposition.

steps: ECG, BP, pH, electrolytes and seizure monitoring with poison centre consultation.
Repeat IV sodium bicarbonate per protocol and monitor pH/sodium/potassium.
Vasopressors for refractory hypotension; benzodiazepines for seizures.
Continue monitoring until QRS and consciousness normalize.
management.safety: Avoid overalkalinisation and hypokalaemia; toxicology sets treatment targets.
management.local: Study guidance only. Follow current emergency department pathways, senior advice, patient factors and verified prescribing references.

stem: A 34-year-old during labour suddenly develops severe hypoxia, hypotension and cardiac arrest. Immediately after ROSC she bleeds profusely from puncture sites and uterus; fibrinogen is 0.7 g/L. There was no drug infusion or anaphylactic rash.
ask: Which diagnosis and response are MOST appropriate?
options: Manage as uterine rupture with emergency laparotomy and packed cells.
Treat suspected amniotic fluid embolism with resuscitation and blood products.
Treat presumed neuraxial hypotension with positioning and fluids.
Treat as severe bronchospasm with adrenaline and inhaled bronchodilators.
Assume septic shock and prioritise broad-spectrum antibiotics alone.
explanations: Uterine rupture can cause haemorrhagic collapse, but it does not readily explain sudden hypoxia followed by profound consumptive coagulopathy and widespread bleeding. Amniotic fluid embolism is the more integrated diagnosis, requiring concurrent resuscitation and DIC management.

Correct: abrupt respiratory and circulatory collapse during labour followed by profound hypofibrinogenaemia and diffuse bleeding is highly suggestive of amniotic fluid embolism with DIC. Continue maternal advanced life support, activate major haemorrhage and obstetric critical-care teams, replace blood products and fibrinogen as guided, and manage uterine haemorrhage.
A vasovagal event may cause brief hypotension or loss of consciousness but does not usually lead to cardiac arrest plus severe bleeding from multiple puncture sites and fibrinogen depletion.
Acute asthma can cause severe hypoxaemia but does not account for abrupt DIC and uterine bleeding. Bronchodilation alone would miss the need for haemorrhage and obstetric resuscitation.

Sepsis can cause DIC, but this presentation is abrupt during labour with cardiopulmonary collapse and immediate coagulopathy, not a progressive infective syndrome. Empirical antibiotics alone would miss urgent bleeding and organ support needs.
pearl: AFE is a clinical diagnosis of sudden peripartum cardiovascular-respiratory collapse and coagulopathy; management is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pivot: Massive PE can resemble AFE but profound early DIC and temporal association with labour can favour AFE.

steps: Immediate ALS with lateral uterine displacement if pregnant, airway/oxygenation and haemodynamic support.
Massive transfusion, fibrinogen replacement and coagulation-guided blood products.
Multidisciplinary obstetrics/anaesthesia/ICU/neonatology and emergency delivery if indicated.
Cardiac/respiratory organ support and delayed complications.
management.safety: Avoid delaying resuscitation to obtain confirmatory imaging; there is no single diagnostic test for AFE.
management.local: Educational sequence. Use current local obstetric/anaesthetic/neonatal protocols, gestational thresholds and multidisciplinary advice.

stem: A 3-month-old with large VSD sweats during feeds, breathes rapidly and has weight gain below expected. Examination shows tachycardia, hepatomegaly and a loud pansystolic murmur. Saturation is 97% on room air.
ask: Which management plan is MOST appropriate?
options: Begin prostaglandin infusion to maintain ductal patency before cardiology review.
Offer feeding advice and monitor growth because the VSD is likely to close.
Start propranolol for tachycardia before defining shunt haemodynamics.
Manage cardiac failure and arrange specialist VSD closure planning.
Give long-term supplemental oxygen to reduce pulmonary arterial pressure.
explanations: Most isolated VSDs are not duct-dependent lesions. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Treat heart failure symptoms, optimise nutrition and refer paediatric cardiology for defect closure planning. A large left-to-right shunt becomes symptomatic after pulmonary vascular resistance falls in infancy.

Small VSDs may close; symptomatic large defects risk failure to thrive/pulmonary hypertension. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Treat heart failure symptoms, optimise nutrition and refer paediatric cardiology for defect closure planning. A large left-to-right shunt becomes symptomatic after pulmonary vascular resistance falls in infancy.

Non-individualised therapy may worsen haemodynamics; anatomy and severity need specialist review. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Treat heart failure symptoms, optimise nutrition and refer paediatric cardiology for defect closure planning. A large left-to-right shunt becomes symptomatic after pulmonary vascular resistance falls in infancy.

Correct: symptomatic large VSD needs diuretic/nutritional support and timely intervention assessment. Clinical distinction: A large left-to-right shunt becomes symptomatic after pulmonary vascular resistance falls in infancy.

Oxygen does not remove shunt volume load and may increase pulmonary blood flow. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Treat heart failure symptoms, optimise nutrition and refer paediatric cardiology for defect closure planning. A large left-to-right shunt becomes symptomatic after pulmonary vascular resistance falls in infancy.
pearl: A large left-to-right shunt becomes symptomatic after pulmonary vascular resistance falls in infancy.
pivot: A tiny restrictive VSD with no growth or haemodynamic problem may need surveillance only.

steps: Work of breathing, feed volume, weight, hepatomegaly and echo anatomy/shunt severity.
Careful diuretics when congested and concentrated feeds/dietetic support.
Paediatric cardiology assessment for closure timing and pulmonary hypertension risk.
Growth, infections, electrolytes and signs of worsening heart failure.
management.safety: Oxygen is not automatically helpful in a child whose main problem is excessive pulmonary blood flow.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

skill: Acute limb compartment syndrome after reperfusion
context: Advanced surgical and acute speciality decisions
stem: A 65-year-old undergoes successful femoral embolectomy for acute limb ischaemia. Four hours later his calf becomes tense with severe pain on passive toe extension, despite a strong palpable pedal pulse. CK is rising.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Arrange urgent fasciotomy assessment for reperfusion compartment syndrome.
Use repeat Doppler ultrasound because palpable pulses exclude critical ischaemia.
Apply compression dressing and elevate the leg to limit postoperative swelling.
Increase analgesia and repeat CK and examination in six hours.
Begin early physiotherapy because the limb has been successfully reperfused.
explanations: Correct: reperfusion swelling can raise compartment pressures despite restored large-artery flow. Clinical distinction: Restored pulses do not rule out reperfusion compartment syndrome; pain on passive stretch is an early alarm.

Pulses may remain present in compartment syndrome, especially after reperfusion. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Urgent surgical fasciotomy assessment for reperfusion-related compartment syndrome. Restored pulses do not rule out reperfusion compartment syndrome; pain on passive stretch is an early alarm.

Compression increases compartment pressure. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Urgent surgical fasciotomy assessment for reperfusion-related compartment syndrome. Restored pulses do not rule out reperfusion compartment syndrome; pain on passive stretch is an early alarm.

Analgesia without decompression can miss irreversible muscle and nerve damage. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Urgent surgical fasciotomy assessment for reperfusion-related compartment syndrome. Restored pulses do not rule out reperfusion compartment syndrome; pain on passive stretch is an early alarm.

Severe acute symptoms after reperfusion are a surgical emergency. In this scenario, the preferred approach is Urgent surgical fasciotomy assessment for reperfusion-related compartment syndrome. Restored pulses do not rule out reperfusion compartment syndrome; pain on passive stretch is an early alarm.
pearl: Restored pulses do not rule out reperfusion compartment syndrome; pain on passive stretch is an early alarm.
pivot: Mild expected reperfusion soreness without tense compartments or neurovascular symptoms may be observed closely.

steps: Serial compartment, sensory, motor and pain exams with immediate vascular/orthopaedic review.
Remove compressive dressings, maintain perfusion and provide analgesia.
Emergency fasciotomy when clinical diagnosis established; assess muscle viability.
CK, electrolytes/potassium, kidney function and urine output for rhabdomyolysis.
management.safety: Do not delay fasciotomy for diagnostic pressure measurements when clinical findings are clear.
management.local: Study summary only: obtain appropriate consultant and multidisciplinary guidance, verified drugs and local operative protocols.

stem: A 44-year-old with metastatic lung cancer develops severe dyspnoea, HR 130/min, BP 78/48 mmHg, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds. Bedside echo shows large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate intervention?
options: Give cautious IV fluid while observing for improvement in chamber filling.
Start vasopressors and schedule elective pericardial window after stabilisation.
Arrange CT staging of the malignant pericardial disease before intervention.
Begin anti-inflammatory medication and serial ultrasound observation.
Perform emergency ultrasound-guided pericardial drainage.
explanations: Cautious fluid may briefly augment preload while preparing drainage, but it is only a bridge and repeat imaging must not defer decompression in a patient with profound hypotension and chamber collapse.

A vasopressor can transiently support perfusion, but scheduling definitive drainage for the next day is unsafe in shock. Tamponade persists until pericardial pressure is relieved; source control takes priority while critical-care support continues.

CT can help define malignant disease in a stable patient, but bedside echocardiography already demonstrates haemodynamically significant tamponade. Transporting an unstable patient for further imaging introduces avoidable risk and delays life-saving drainage.

Anti-inflammatory therapy can be useful in selected inflammatory pericardial syndromes, but not as immediate treatment for malignant tamponade with shock. Serial echo without drainage would allow impaired filling to persist.

Correct: obstructive shock from malignant pericardial effusion needs immediate specialist-performed image-guided pericardiocentesis or appropriate surgical drainage, with monitoring, airway planning and temporising resuscitation in parallel. Send fluid for cytology and discuss recurrence management after stabilisation.
pearl: Tamponade causes obstructive shock; pericardial drainage, not diuresis, reverses physiology.
pivot: A small asymptomatic effusion without chamber collapse is usually monitored/etiologically assessed.

steps: Activate emergency, cardiology and critical-care teams; monitor ECG, blood pressure and oxygenation and establish IV access.
Arrange emergency ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis by an experienced team, or surgical drainage if anatomy/etiology requires it.
Use judicious IV fluid and vasopressors only as indicated while organising drainage. Plan airway support carefully because positive-pressure ventilation can worsen preload dependence.
Send pericardial fluid for indicated analysis including cytology, reassess haemodynamics and echo, and plan malignant-effusion recurrence prevention with oncology/cardiology.
management.safety: In malignant tamponade with shock, fluids and vasopressors are not definitive; delaying drainage can be fatal.
management.local: Checked against ESC 2025 pericardial disease guidance; follow local specialist pathways.

context: Advanced GP psychiatry ethics and safe prescribing
stem: A 29-year-old taking clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia reports fever 38.9°C, sore throat and oral ulcers. His absolute neutrophil count has fallen to 0.3 × 10^9/L from 2.4 one month ago. He is tachycardic but normotensive.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Withhold clozapine and urgently investigate febrile neutropenia.
Repeat the ANC before starting antibiotics or withholding clozapine.
Continue clozapine at reduced dose while monitoring daily ANC.
Switch temporarily to another antipsychotic while neutropenia is assessed.
Start mouth care and antiviral treatment for suspected viral stomatitis.
explanations: Correct: ANC 0.3 ×10⁹/L with fever and mucosal infection symptoms during clozapine treatment is a medical emergency. Withhold clozapine, urgently admit, obtain cultures without delaying broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and involve haematology and the treating psychiatric service; monitor for sepsis and discuss specialist haematological support.

Severe neutropenia with fever is a medical emergency: waiting for a confirmatory count before stopping clozapine or starting indicated empiric antibiotics risks sepsis progression. Stop clozapine, assess and treat immediately.
Continuing the suspected causative drug in severe neutropenia risks progressive marrow suppression and potentially fatal infection. A one-month delay in repeat testing is unsafe.

Substituting another antipsychotic may later be needed for relapse prevention, but the priority is the drug-related agranulocytosis and potential infection. Immediate clozapine interruption and emergency medical care cannot be deferred.

Oral ulcers can result from profound neutropenia and infection; treating them as simple viral stomatitis would miss a potentially life-threatening drug adverse effect. Arrange febrile-neutropenia treatment urgently.
pearl: Clozapine monitoring thresholds protect against agranulocytosis; fever or sore throat warrants immediate blood counts and urgent assessment.
pivot: Mild ANC reduction without symptoms follows a different monitoring/action threshold under local clozapine register.

steps: Withhold clozapine under monitoring-program rules and contact treating psychiatry.
Emergency cultures, IV antipseudomonal antibiotics per febrile-neutropenia pathway and admission.
Haematology review for G-CSF and repeated full blood counts.
Alternative antipsychotic/rechallenge decisions require specialist multidisciplinary review.
management.safety: Do not assume infection is simple tonsillitis in a patient with ANC under 0.5.
management.local: Educational teaching, not individual clinical orders. Apply current local mental health law, safeguarding procedures and medication monitoring requirements.

stem: A 28-year-old presents with sudden palpitations. Monitor shows regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 184/min. She is alert, BP 126/74 mmHg, no chest pain and SpO2 99%. No known structural heart disease or asthma.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate first active treatment?
options: Try modified Valsalva, followed by IV adenosine if unsuccessful.
Give IV adenosine before attempting a vagal manoeuvre in this stable patient.
Start IV diltiazem without a preceding attempt to terminate vagally.
Perform synchronised cardioversion immediately despite stable perfusion.
Prescribe oral beta blockade and arrange outpatient ECG reassessment.
explanations: Correct: vagal manoeuvres are preferred first active therapy in stable regular AV-node-dependent SVT. Clinical distinction: Management of tachyarrhythmia begins with haemodynamic stability and QRS width/regularity, not simply the heart rate.

Adenosine is appropriate if vagal manoeuvres fail and rhythm characteristics permit, but modified Valsalva is the first active measure for a stable regular narrow-complex SVT. Adenosine requires a monitored setting and rapid IV administration.

An AV-nodal blocker such as diltiazem may be an alternative in selected stable SVTs, but it is not the first manoeuvre when vagal treatment and adenosine are available. Confirm rhythm and contraindications before drug selection.

Synchronised cardioversion is indicated for haemodynamic instability or refractory tachycardia. With normal BP, alertness and no ischaemic symptoms, start with a modified Valsalva and escalate if unsuccessful.
Longer-term beta blockade may help recurrent episodes, but she has an active tachycardia at 184/min requiring immediate assessment and termination, not an unmonitored outpatient plan.
pearl: Management of tachyarrhythmia begins with haemodynamic stability and QRS width/regularity, not simply the heart rate.
pivot: If shock, ischaemic chest pain or pulmonary oedema develops, synchronised cardioversion becomes urgent.

steps: Try modified Valsalva, followed by IV adenosine if unsuccessful.
Modified Valsalva with supine reposition and leg raise where appropriate.
Rapid IV adenosine via proximal cannula with flush and continuous ECG if rhythm suitable; prepare for transient AV block and discuss contraindications.
Alternative drugs or synchronised cardioversion under specialist guidance if refractory or unstable.
management.safety: Avoid AV-nodal blockers for irregular wide-complex pre-excited AF; assess rhythm carefully before adenosine.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 28-year-old on postoperative day 3 after emergency Caesarean develops temperature 39 °C, tachycardia, uterine fundal tenderness and foul-smelling lochia. Incision is clean and there is no respiratory or urinary complaint.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate treatment?
options: Begin oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and reassess in hospital the next morning.
Give IV fluids and obtain endometrial cultures before starting antibiotics.
Arrange pelvic ultrasound before treating presumed retained products.
Give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics for post-Caesarean endometritis.
Give IV metronidazole alone and reassess fever after the first dose.
explanations: Oral therapy can be considered for selected mild outpatient infections but not a febrile, tachycardic patient three days after Caesarean with fundal tenderness and foul lochia. She needs inpatient broad-spectrum IV coverage and evaluation.

Resuscitation and cultures are reasonable in parallel, but waiting on specimens before antibiotics delays treatment of likely post-Caesarean endometritis. Empiric coverage should address mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms.

Ultrasound may help if retained tissue, abscess or persistent symptoms are suspected, but the clinical syndrome already supports postpartum endometritis. Imaging should not postpone first-line IV antimicrobial treatment.

Correct: post-Caesarean endometritis is polymicrobial and should be treated promptly with broad IV coverage. Clinical distinction: Postpartum endometritis is often diagnosed clinically from fever, uterine tenderness and abnormal lochia, particularly post-Caesarean.
Metronidazole provides anaerobic cover, but endometritis is polymicrobial and also requires coverage of relevant aerobic organisms. Use an appropriate IV broad-spectrum regimen and monitor response.
pearl: Postpartum endometritis is often diagnosed clinically from fever, uterine tenderness and abnormal lochia, particularly post-Caesarean.
pivot: If fever persists despite adequate therapy, evaluate retained products, abscess, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis or another source.

steps: Give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics for post-Caesarean endometritis.
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic coverage (e.g. locally approved clindamycin–gentamicin regimen or alternative), plus fluids and analgesia.
Monitor fever, haemodynamics and uterine tenderness; consider ultrasound if retained tissue/abscess suspected.
Senior O&G review and source control if refractory or complicated infection.
management.safety: Choice of antibiotics depends on allergy, renal function, antimicrobial guidance and breastfeeding considerations.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 47-year-old taking frequent NSAIDs develops sudden severe epigastric pain followed by a rigid, diffusely tender abdomen. Upright chest X-ray shows free subdiaphragmatic air. BP 96/58 mmHg and pulse 118/min.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give IV fluids, antibiotics and PPI while waiting for pain to settle before referral.
Perform urgent diagnostic endoscopy to visualise the ulcer before calling surgery.
Order repeat abdominal radiography after fluids to confirm persistent free air.
Use high-dose IV PPI and nasogastric decompression as definitive treatment.
Resuscitate and arrange emergency surgery for perforated ulcer.
explanations: IV fluids, antibiotics and PPI are appropriate initial components but cannot treat a free perforation with a rigid abdomen and shock physiology alone. Emergency surgical assessment and source control must be arranged simultaneously.
Endoscopy is not the initial procedure for suspected perforated peptic ulcer with peritonism; insufflation may aggravate perforation, and operative source control is time-sensitive.
Free subdiaphragmatic air plus an acute rigid abdomen is compelling evidence of perforation. Waiting for repeat imaging adds little and delays resuscitation and surgical management.

Selected contained perforations in highly stable patients may be managed non-operatively under strict conditions. This patient has diffuse peritoneal signs and physiological compromise, making conservative care unsuitable.

Correct: treat sepsis/peritoneal contamination and obtain definitive surgical control. Clinical distinction: Free intraperitoneal air plus generalised peritonitis is a surgical emergency; resuscitation and antibiotics happen before and during theatre.
pearl: Free intraperitoneal air plus generalised peritonitis is a surgical emergency; resuscitation and antibiotics happen before and during theatre.
pivot: A small sealed perforation in a stable carefully selected patient may have non-operative management under specialist observation.

steps: Resuscitate and arrange emergency surgery for perforated ulcer.
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for enteric contamination, IV PPI, nasogastric decompression where indicated.
Urgent surgery for closure/repair and peritoneal washout; H. pylori/NSAID risk treatment after recovery.
Sepsis, leak, renal function and postoperative nutrition monitoring.
management.safety: Avoid delays from unnecessary investigations when imaging already shows free air and clinical peritonitis.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 38-year-old with schizophrenia is admitted after abruptly becoming mute and motionless for 18 hours. She maintains unusual postures and exhibits waxy flexibility and negativism. Temp 36.8 °C, HR 88/min and CK normal. She is not eating or drinking.
ask: What is the BEST immediate treatment approach?
options: Give IV fluids and observe for spontaneous reversal before treating rigidity.
Start high-dose haloperidol to suppress the motor and behavioural syndrome.
Treat as delirium with an anticholinergic while waiting for psychiatric review.
Give monitored lorazepam for catatonia and assess for ECT.
Start immediate ECT without assessing hydration, nutrition or physical stability.
explanations: IV fluid and nutrition support are important because the patient is not eating or drinking, but they do not replace direct treatment of catatonia. A monitored lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and may increase risk of malignant catatonia/NMS in vulnerable patients. Waxy flexibility, negativism and immobility are not reasons to escalate haloperidol automatically.

Delirium should be assessed as a potential cause or comorbidity, but anticholinergics can worsen confusion and do not treat classic catatonic motor signs. Assess medical causes and trial a benzodiazepine under observation.

Correct: benzodiazepines are first-line for catatonia; failure or severe illness may need ECT. Clinical distinction: Recognise mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility and negativism as catatonia; assess hydration, immobility complications and underlying cause.

ECT is highly effective in severe or benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and may be urgent in malignant presentations. The initial pathway still includes medical assessment and stabilisation alongside lorazepam when appropriate.
pearl: Recognise mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility and negativism as catatonia; assess hydration, immobility complications and underlying cause.
pivot: Fever, autonomic instability and CK rise raise concern for malignant catatonia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome with immediate ICU/ECT pathways.

steps: Give monitored lorazepam for catatonia and assess for ECT.
Monitored lorazepam challenge followed by scheduled benzodiazepine if responsive; plan ECT for nonresponse or severe case.
IV/NG fluids/nutrition as needed, VTE prophylaxis when appropriate, pressure care and monitoring for infection/CK elevation.
Review dopamine antagonists and other precipitants with psychiatry.
management.safety: Do not escalate antipsychotics reflexively in active catatonia; malignant catatonia needs urgent specialist treatment.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 60-year-old is rescued from a frozen lake. Core temperature is 25.6°C, GCS 5 and the monitor shows a very slow wide-complex rhythm. No obvious breathing is detected in five seconds. Rescuers cannot feel a pulse immediately.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next action?
options: Check the central pulse carefully and begin hypothermia resuscitation.
Begin conventional CPR immediately after a five-second peripheral pulse check.
Give repeated defibrillation shocks before confirming a shockable rhythm.
Use vigorous limb rubbing and active exercise to generate heat rapidly.
Delay airway support until the core temperature rises above 30°C.
explanations: Correct: prevent false arrest diagnosis, handle gently and treat according to hypothermic ALS modifications. Clinical distinction: In profound hypothermia, slow circulation can mimic arrest; check centrally for up to a minute and use modified resuscitation rules.

Severe hypothermia can cause profound bradycardia and an extremely slow, weak pulse. A careful central pulse assessment for up to about a minute prevents inappropriate chest compressions in someone who still has circulation, while resuscitation should begin if arrest is confirmed.

The monitor shows a slow wide-complex rhythm, not established VF/pulseless VT. Shock treatment depends on rhythm and arrest status, with modifications for low core temperature according to resuscitation guidance.
Rough handling and vigorous limb movement can trigger dangerous dysrhythmias in profound hypothermia. Handle gently, insulate, prevent further heat loss and begin controlled rewarming.

Airway and ventilatory support are assessed immediately using a hypothermia-adapted approach. Delaying management solely because the patient remains below 30°C can worsen hypoxia and circulatory compromise.
pearl: In profound hypothermia, slow circulation can mimic arrest; check centrally for up to a minute and use modified resuscitation rules.
pivot: Mild hypothermia in an alert stable person can be managed with passive warming and observation.

steps: Check the central pulse carefully and begin hypothermia resuscitation.
Prevent further heat loss, monitor rhythm, warm oxygen/fluids and avoid rough movement.
Consult critical-care/ECMO-capable centre for very severe instability or arrest.
Defibrillation and adrenaline dosing may require hypothermia-specific modifications.
management.safety: Never assume death before an appropriate hypothermia resuscitation assessment.
management.local: Study guidance only. Follow current emergency department pathways, senior advice, patient factors and verified prescribing references.

stem: Immediately after placental delivery a woman develops severe abdominal pain, heavy bleeding and shock. A smooth red mass is visible at the introitus, and the uterine fundus cannot be palpated abdominally.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
options: Administer uterotonics immediately to contract the uterus before replacement.
Call for help and replace the acutely inverted uterus.
Apply sustained fundal pressure from the abdomen while arranging ultrasound.
Proceed to hysterectomy before attempting manual reduction or resuscitation.
Apply traction to the visible uterine mass to bring the fundus down further.
explanations: Uterotonics before reduction can make the constriction ring tighten and render replacement harder. Call for senior assistance, treat shock, replace the inverted uterus promptly, then give uterotonics once normal position is restored.

Correct: acute uterine inversion causes postpartum haemorrhage and shock. Activate obstetric and anaesthetic emergency response, initiate resuscitation and blood products as indicated, and urgently attempt manual uterine replacement by an experienced clinician. Uterotonics are generally given after successful replacement to prevent reinversion.

The uterine fundus is absent abdominally and a red mass is visible at the introitus, strongly suggesting inversion rather than atony. External pressure alone is not the standard emergency reduction method.

Hysterectomy is reserved for rare irreducible or uncontrolled cases after appropriate escalation. Immediate resuscitation and prompt manual replacement offer the fastest chance of correcting the acute inversion.
Traction can worsen inversion and tissue injury. Stop any cord traction and seek skilled prompt reduction while addressing haemorrhage and shock.
pearl: Uterine inversion causes massive PPH and neurogenic shock; replace the uterus first, then restore tone.
pivot: Uterine atony causes a boggy palpable abdominal fundus, not a mass through the cervix with absent fundus.

steps: Call for help and replace the acutely inverted uterus.
Immediate manual Johnson manoeuvre by experienced obstetrician; consider tocolysis/anaesthesia if difficult.
Give uterotonics to maintain contraction, treat bleeding, check placenta and injuries.
Surgical replacement if manual reduction fails; manage DIC/shock.
management.safety: Do not remove an attached placenta before repositioning unless obstetric expertise directs; may worsen bleeding.
management.local: Educational sequence. Use current local obstetric/anaesthetic/neonatal protocols, gestational thresholds and multidisciplinary advice.

stem: A 6-week-old has inspiratory stridor that is louder when supine and during feeding but quietens when prone or upright. He is afebrile, SpO2 99%, feeding adequately and gaining weight. No cyanotic events.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Arrange urgent supraglottoplasty for all stridor persisting beyond four weeks.
Begin anti-reflux medication as sole treatment and avoid airway review.
Monitor feeding and growth in likely laryngomalacia with ENT review.
Admit for continuous oxygen because positional stridor predicts hypoxaemia.
Perform emergency intubation despite normal oxygenation and growth.
explanations: Supraglottoplasty is considered for severe laryngomalacia with failure to thrive, significant obstruction, cyanosis or similar concerns. Mild positional stridor with good growth is generally managed conservatively.

Reflux management may be considered for associated symptoms but does not replace assessment of stridor and growth. Appropriate ENT evaluation and safety-net advice are needed if feeding or breathing worsens.

Correct: positional early-infant stridor with normal growth is often benign but needs surveillance. Clinical distinction: Laryngomalacia stridor worsens supine/feeding and improves upright; poor weight gain or apnoea changes urgency.

Observation and sometimes monitoring may be required for apnoea, desaturation or feeding failure. A well infant with normal SpO2 and weight gain does not automatically require admission solely for positional inspiratory noise.

Intubation is an emergency response to critical airway compromise, not a routine intervention for stable mild laryngomalacia. Escalate urgently if cyanosis, marked work of breathing or feeding failure develops.
pearl: Laryngomalacia stridor worsens supine/feeding and improves upright; poor weight gain or apnoea changes urgency.
pivot: Stridor at rest with drooling and acute febrile toxicity signals dangerous supraglottic infection instead.

steps: Monitor feeding and growth in likely laryngomalacia with ENT review.
Feeding posture, reflux assessment if clinically significant, avoid unnecessary treatment.
ENT flexible nasendoscopy for confirmation/atypical features; specialist surgery for severe failure to thrive or hypoxaemia.
Return for apnoea, persistent retractions, blue spells or faltering growth.
management.safety: Do not dismiss worsening inspiratory obstruction solely because oxygen saturation was once normal.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

context: Advanced surgical and acute speciality decisions
stem: A 62-year-old has upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, lipase eight times normal, jaundice, fever 39.2°C and BP 90/55 mmHg. Ultrasound shows common bile duct dilation and a distal stone.
ask: Which treatment component is MOST time-critical beyond resuscitation and antibiotics?
options: Arrange urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy without biliary duct decompression.
Treat with IV antibiotics alone and reassess the stone after the fever settles.
Decompress the gallbladder percutaneously without addressing the common duct.
Arrange early pancreatic necrosectomy to remove the cause of systemic illness.
Perform urgent ERCP for acute cholangitis with obstruction.
explanations: Cholecystectomy reduces recurrent gallstone events after stabilisation, but severe cholangitis from an obstructed common bile duct needs urgent drainage. Removing the gallbladder alone may not relieve the CBD obstruction.
IV antibiotics are essential but may not control infection in a persistently obstructed biliary system. Early ERCP provides drainage and source control in cholangitis with hypotension and jaundice.
Percutaneous cholecystostomy can help selected critically ill patients with acute cholecystitis. It does not reliably drain an obstructed distal common bile duct causing ascending cholangitis.
Necrosectomy is not an early intervention for ordinary gallstone pancreatitis and there is no described infected pancreatic necrosis. The immediate source of sepsis is the obstructed biliary tree.

Correct: acute biliary pancreatitis with concurrent cholangitis/obstruction needs prompt duct drainage. Clinical distinction: ERCP is not indicated in every gallstone pancreatitis, but concurrent cholangitis is a major indication.
pearl: ERCP is not indicated in every gallstone pancreatitis, but concurrent cholangitis is a major indication.
pivot: Mild gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis/obstruction generally needs supportive care and index-admission cholecystectomy.

steps: Perform urgent ERCP for acute cholangitis with obstruction.
Urgent biliary ERCP after appropriate resuscitation.
Broad IV antibiotics then culture-directed step-down.
management.safety: Do not confuse sterile pancreatic inflammation with obstructed infected bile.
management.local: Study summary only: obtain appropriate consultant and multidisciplinary guidance, verified drugs and local operative protocols.

stem: A 57-year-old taking loop diuretics develops weakness and palpitations. K is 2.1 mmol/L, magnesium 0.42 mmol/L and ECG shows prominent U waves with ventricular ectopics. Kidney function is normal.
ask: Which immediate treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Replace potassium orally and recheck the ECG after several hours of observation.
Replace IV potassium under monitoring but defer magnesium replacement.
Replace IV potassium and magnesium with cardiac monitoring.
Give IV magnesium first, withhold potassium until ventricular ectopy resolves.
Prescribe a potassium-sparing diuretic and repeat electrolytes tomorrow.
explanations: Oral potassium is suitable for many mild or moderate cases, but K 2.1 mmol/L with ventricular ectopy is high-risk and needs monitored rapid correction. Severe magnesium deficiency also requires treatment.
IV potassium is needed, but magnesium 0.42 mmol/L can perpetuate renal potassium wasting and arrhythmias. Both should be replaced with close biochemical and ECG monitoring.

Correct: life-threatening hypokalaemia with ECG changes requires carefully controlled parenteral correction. Clinical distinction: Magnesium depletion makes hypokalaemia refractory until both are corrected.

Magnesium correction is important, but withholding potassium in severe symptomatic hypokalaemia leaves immediate electrical instability untreated. Replace both using appropriate safe infusion protocols.

Changing chronic diuretic treatment may prevent recurrence but cannot address acute ventricular ectopy and marked electrolyte depletion. The immediate priority is controlled IV replacement and monitoring.
pearl: Magnesium depletion makes hypokalaemia refractory until both are corrected.
pivot: Mild asymptomatic hypokalaemia can often be treated orally and medication-adjusted.

steps: Replace IV potassium and magnesium with cardiac monitoring.
Monitored diluted IV KCl at protocol-approved rate/concentration and correct Mg.
Frequent serum K/Mg and ECG, adjust for renal function.
Modify causative medications and arrange follow-up electrolyte checks.
management.safety: Never administer IV potassium as undiluted push.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

context: Advanced GP psychiatry ethics and safe prescribing
stem: A 35-year-old with daily heroin use has relapsed multiple times after short detoxification programmes and suffered one nonfatal overdose. He asks for 'something that stops cravings' and wants to continue working. He is not intoxicated and has capacity.
ask: Which strategy has the strongest evidence for reducing overdose and improving retention?
options: Offer a further short inpatient detoxification programme without maintenance.
Start extended-release naltrexone immediately while current opioid use continues.
Provide overdose education and take-home naloxone as the only intervention.
Offer methadone or buprenorphine maintenance with psychosocial support.
Use scheduled supervised withdrawal each month rather than ongoing treatment.
explanations: Detoxification may be part of an individual care plan, but repeated withdrawal without maintenance has high relapse and overdose risk. Opioid agonist treatment improves retention and reduces mortality.

Naltrexone is an option for selected patients after full detoxification; starting it while physically opioid dependent may precipitate withdrawal. It does not have the same broad retention evidence as methadone/buprenorphine in this repeated-relapse scenario.
Take-home naloxone is important harm reduction, especially after an overdose, but it does not treat dependence or cravings. Combine overdose prevention with evidence-based maintenance treatment.

Correct: opioid agonist maintenance lowers mortality and improves retention compared with repeated detox alone. Clinical distinction: Evidence-based OUD care includes agonist maintenance, harm reduction, naloxone, infection care and psychological support.

Scheduled withdrawal alone does not provide sustained protection from cravings and overdose for someone repeatedly relapsing after detoxification. Ongoing opioid agonist maintenance is more effective at retention and harm reduction.
pearl: Evidence-based OUD care includes agonist maintenance, harm reduction, naloxone, infection care and psychological support.
pivot: Some patients prefer antagonist therapy after full detox, but it requires careful induction and engagement.

steps: Offer methadone or buprenorphine maintenance with psychosocial support.
Offer buprenorphine or methadone via accredited service with correct induction and titration.
Take-home naloxone, safer-use education, hepatitis/HIV testing and vaccination.
Peer support, counselling, social needs, long-term follow-up.
management.safety: Buprenorphine started before adequate withdrawal can precipitate withdrawal; specialist induction pathways matter.
management.local: Educational teaching, not individual clinical orders. Apply current local mental health law, safeguarding procedures and medication monitoring requirements.

stem: A 67-year-old with severe hypertension develops sudden dyspnoea and pink frothy sputum. BP 206/112 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 80% despite nasal oxygen, diffuse crackles and marked distress. He remains conscious and cooperative.
ask: Which immediate strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: Give IV furosemide first, assessing respiratory support after diuresis begins.
Start non-invasive ventilation and IV nitrates if haemodynamics allow.
Use high-flow oxygen alone and await a bedside echo before vasodilation.
Start IV beta blockade to lower BP before addressing respiratory distress.
Give a crystalloid challenge before nitrates because tachycardia implies hypovolaemia.
explanations: IV diuretics can help volume overload, but hypertensive flash pulmonary oedema with marked hypoxaemia needs immediate respiratory support. Non-invasive ventilation and vasodilators can rapidly reduce work of breathing and pulmonary congestion.

Correct: hypertensive cardiogenic pulmonary oedema needs rapid oxygenation/ventilatory support and afterload reduction. Clinical distinction: In acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with severe hypertension, NIV plus rapidly acting vasodilators may relieve distress quickly while diuresis removes excess fluid.
Oxygen is essential, but profound hypoxaemia and distress despite standard oxygen favour early positive-pressure support. Echo is useful after stabilisation but should not delay treatment.

Reducing cardiac workload matters, but IV beta blockade is not the immediate strategy during acute decompensated pulmonary oedema and may worsen pump failure. Controlled vasodilation and NIV are more appropriate with severe hypertension.
Pink frothy sputum, diffuse crackles and severe hypertension indicate hydrostatic lung oedema, not hypovolaemia. Large fluid loading would aggravate pulmonary congestion.
pearl: In acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with severe hypertension, NIV plus rapidly acting vasodilators may relieve distress quickly while diuresis removes excess fluid.
pivot: If severely hypotensive with cool peripheries, avoid nitrates and manage potential cardiogenic shock with critical-care input.

steps: Start non-invasive ventilation and IV nitrates if haemodynamics allow.
Titrated nitrates if BP supports it and IV loop diuretic where overloaded; avoid routine opioids.
ECG/troponin, arrhythmia, BP, chest imaging, renal function and echo; reassess cardiogenic versus non-cardiogenic cause.
Frequent SpO2, RR, consciousness, BP and urine output.
management.safety: NIV requires monitoring and cooperation; altered consciousness, inability to protect airway or worsening shock may mandate intubation.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 33-year-old at 31 weeks presents with painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. She has no contractions, BP 120/76 mmHg and fetal heart rate is reassuring. A scan at 20 weeks showed a low-lying anterior placenta.
ask: Which immediate assessment is MOST appropriate?
options: Perform speculum assessment before ultrasound to locate the cervix and bleeding.
Perform maternal–fetal assessment and ultrasound before vaginal examination.
Use digital cervical examination immediately to determine labour progression.
Observe on the ward without imaging because maternal and fetal vitals are normal.
Give tocolysis to prevent contractions before identifying the bleeding source.
explanations: A gentle speculum exam may be appropriate once clinically safe, but placental position should be established by ultrasound before potentially hazardous vaginal examinations in suspected placenta praevia. Maternal and fetal stability remain the first assessment priorities.

Correct: suspected placenta praevia requires safe evaluation without digital vaginal exam. Clinical distinction: Painless antepartum bleeding with prior low placenta suggests placenta praevia until proven otherwise: NO digital vaginal exam.
A digital vaginal examination can disrupt a placenta covering or near the internal os and cause severe haemorrhage. It should be avoided until previa is excluded by imaging.

Stable observations do not make third-trimester bleeding benign. Assessment should include maternal haemodynamics, fetal status and placental localisation, with readiness to escalate if bleeding increases.
Without contractions, tocolysis does not address the cause and can mask or delay necessary assessment. Confirm placental location and fetal well-being first.
pearl: Painless antepartum bleeding with prior low placenta suggests placenta praevia until proven otherwise: NO digital vaginal exam.
pivot: Painful bleeding with a tender hypertonic uterus suggests placental abruption, which may have concealed blood loss.

steps: Perform maternal–fetal assessment and ultrasound before vaginal examination.
Transabdominal and/or transvaginal ultrasound safely determines placental relation to cervix.
Senior obstetric review; anti-D when indicated, antenatal steroids if preterm birth risk and timing/location of delivery based on ongoing bleeding.
management.safety: Never perform digital vaginal exam in suspected placenta praevia before imaging.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 49-year-old with alcohol-related acute pancreatitis has persistent abdominal pain and raised inflammatory markers on day 4. CT shows pancreatic necrosis but no gas in collections. She is afebrile, haemodynamically stable and has no cultures suggesting infection.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Start antibiotics because the presence of any pancreatic necrosis implies infection.
Keep her nil by mouth until necrosis resolves on CT imaging.
Arrange early endoscopic drainage of all necrotic collections on day four.
Begin prophylactic antifungal therapy because high CRP predicts fungal necrosis.
Provide supportive pancreatitis care without prophylactic antibiotics.
explanations: Pancreatic necrosis may be sterile. Antibiotics are appropriate for confirmed or strongly suspected infection or another source, not solely for a CT appearance without fever, gas or sepsis.
Early enteral nutrition is generally preferred when feasible in acute pancreatitis. Prolonged bowel rest is not routine therapy for stable sterile necrosis and may worsen nutritional outcomes.

Intervention is reserved for infected or symptomatic collections under appropriate timing and expertise, usually deferred until maturation when possible. Day-four stable sterile necrosis does not warrant routine drainage.
Inflammation and raised CRP alone do not prove fungal infection or justify antifungal prophylaxis. Monitor for clinical deterioration and treat a demonstrated infection.

Correct: sterile necrosis needs organ support and monitoring, not routine antimicrobial treatment. Clinical distinction: Pancreatic necrosis can be sterile. Treat infected necrosis with antibiotics and appropriately timed drainage/source control, but do not prophylax sterile tissue.
pearl: Pancreatic necrosis can be sterile. Treat infected necrosis with antibiotics and appropriately timed drainage/source control, but do not prophylax sterile tissue.
pivot: If gas, bacteraemia, sepsis or clinical deterioration suggests infected necrosis, start targeted antibiotics and discuss step-up drainage.

steps: Provide supportive pancreatitis care without prophylactic antibiotics.
Judicious fluids, adequate analgesia, early oral/enteral nutrition as tolerated and thromboprophylaxis when safe.
Look for fever, gas in collection, bacteraemia or new organ dysfunction; delay invasive intervention for sterile stable necrosis.
Multidisciplinary step-up drainage/necrosectomy for infected or symptomatic collections.
management.safety: Routine prophylactic carbapenems and early necrosectomy are not indicated in stable sterile necrosis.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 27-year-old reports sudden distressing images of harming her baby, which she finds abhorrent and inconsistent with her beliefs. She avoids knives and repeatedly seeks reassurance. She has never wanted to harm the infant, recognises thoughts are her own and has no hallucinations or fixed delusions.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Admit for assessment of postpartum psychosis before attempting OCD-focused care.
Use close infant supervision as the sole intervention until thoughts stop.
Offer reassurance and psychoeducation without formal risk or mental-state review.
Offer CBT with exposure/response prevention and consider an SSRI.
Treat with an antipsychotic first because the content involves infant harm.
explanations: Urgent assessment is warranted if psychotic features or intent emerge, but ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts with intact insight and avoidance are more suggestive of perinatal OCD. Automatic psychosis labelling may increase distress and stigma.

Supportive supervision can form part of a safety plan when indicated, but does not treat the obsession-compulsion cycle. An individualised risk evaluation followed by evidence-based therapy is needed.

Compassionate explanation that intrusive thoughts can be ego-dystonic is helpful, yet assessment remains essential, and persistent significant distress warrants structured treatment rather than reassurance alone.

Correct: harm obsessions respond to ERP and serotonergic treatment, with proportionate risk assessment. Clinical distinction: Unwanted ego-dystonic harm thoughts with reassurance seeking and avoidance suggest OCD; command hallucinations or delusional intent change urgency.

Antipsychotics are not first-line for OCD solely because the images are violent. The patient recognises them as unwanted and implausible; ERP-based CBT, with an SSRI when appropriate, targets the mechanism.
pearl: Unwanted ego-dystonic harm thoughts with reassurance seeking and avoidance suggest OCD; command hallucinations or delusional intent change urgency.
pivot: If the patient believes an external voice commands harming the infant or acts on the belief, consider psychotic disorder/postpartum psychosis and safeguarding.

steps: Offer CBT with exposure/response prevention and consider an SSRI.
Offer structured CBT with ERP; consider SSRI when indicated, including perinatal risk–benefit discussion.
Address avoidance, sleep, family reassurance cycles and monitor functioning and symptom severity.
management.safety: Avoid assuming all intrusive harm obsessions indicate dangerousness, but do not omit infant safety assessment.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 33-year-old receives a high-voltage electrical shock at work and falls. There are small entry and exit burns, severe forearm pain and swelling, dark urine and ECG shows frequent ventricular ectopy. BP is currently 110/68 mmHg.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate management bundle?
options: Monitor ECG and evaluate trauma, rhabdomyolysis and compartment syndrome.
Give IV fluids and urine monitoring but defer ECG telemetry if BP remains normal.
Treat the entry burns and delay limb assessment until creatine kinase returns.
Focus on arrhythmia monitoring and defer a trauma survey without visible fractures.
Perform immediate fasciotomy in all high-voltage shocks despite no pressure assessment.
explanations: Correct: hidden electrical tissue injury and arrhythmia risk mandate inpatient care. Clinical distinction: High-voltage injury is about current path and deep damage, not surface burn area.
Rhabdomyolysis care includes appropriate IV fluids and renal/electrolyte monitoring, but documented ventricular ectopy makes ECG monitoring essential even when BP is initially normal.
Small cutaneous burns can conceal deep muscle injury. Progressive forearm pain and swelling require urgent compartment evaluation, and dark urine suggests myoglobinuria even before CK results.

Arrhythmia monitoring is appropriate, but high-voltage exposure with a fall can produce fractures, occult trauma, deep burns and compartment syndrome. A full trauma and limb assessment cannot be omitted.

Fasciotomy may be urgently required when compartment syndrome is clinically established, but is not performed automatically after every electrical injury. Assess evolving pain, neurovascular function and pressures when indicated.
pearl: High-voltage injury is about current path and deep damage, not surface burn area.
pivot: A low-voltage household exposure with normal ECG, no symptoms and no trauma may be suitable for discharge per local policy.

steps: Monitor ECG and evaluate trauma, rhabdomyolysis and compartment syndrome.
CK, potassium, renal tests, urinalysis and serial limb neurovascular/compartment assessments.
Titrated isotonic fluids for rhabdomyolysis while watching urine output and overload.
Burns, cardiology, orthopaedics/vascular input for significant injury.
management.safety: Hyperkalaemia and compartment syndrome may develop despite reassuring early skin examination.
management.local: Study guidance only. Follow current emergency department pathways, senior advice, patient factors and verified prescribing references.

stem: A 32-year-old at 35 weeks with a documented velamentous cord insertion has spontaneous rupture of membranes followed immediately by bright-red bleeding. Maternal BP is normal, but fetal heart rate falls to 60/min and remains there.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Start corticosteroids and observe fetal heart rate for 24 hours if bleeding stops.
Perform a speculum examination to confirm fetal-vessel rupture before theatre.
Proceed to emergency Caesarean delivery for ruptured vasa praevia.
Apply tocolysis to delay delivery until 37 weeks if maternal BP is stable.
Induce vaginal delivery quickly because maternal haemodynamics are normal.
explanations: Antenatal steroids help preterm lung maturation when delivery can be safely delayed, but sustained fetal bradycardia after membrane rupture and bleeding is an immediate emergency. Waiting exposes the fetus to fatal haemorrhage.
Clinical suspicion is already very high with velamentous vessels, post-ROM bleeding and fetal bradycardia. Speculum examination must not delay emergency delivery.

Correct: fetal vessels can bleed rapidly despite maternal stability and require immediate birth. Clinical distinction: Painless bleeding at membrane rupture with acute fetal bradycardia is vasa praevia until excluded, especially with velamentous insertion.
Fetal compromise in suspected vasa praevia is not amenable to tocolysis. Urgent birth is needed despite maternal stability because the bleeding may be fetal.
Maternal observations may remain normal during massive fetal blood loss. Vaginal induction is too slow with persistent FHR 60/min; emergency Caesarean offers the quickest rescue.
pearl: Painless bleeding at membrane rupture with acute fetal bradycardia is vasa praevia until excluded, especially with velamentous insertion.
pivot: Placenta praevia causes maternal bleeding, whereas vasa praevia rupture may devastate fetus while mother stays stable.

steps: Proceed to emergency Caesarean delivery for ruptured vasa praevia.
Maternal ABC, IV access, fetal monitoring and rapid theatre transfer.
Neonatal assessment for acute anaemia/hypovolaemia and transfusion if required.
management.safety: Do not wait for maternal shock; the fetus can exsanguinate in minutes.
management.local: Educational sequence. Use current local obstetric/anaesthetic/neonatal protocols, gestational thresholds and multidisciplinary advice.

stem: A 7-week-old has frequent paroxysms of cough ending in brief apnoea and cyanosis. Immunisations are not yet complete. An older sibling has a prolonged cough. The infant is afebrile, but SpO2 drops during episodes.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Arrange PCR testing and observe at home because there is no fever.
Give macrolide therapy but defer admission unless pneumonia develops.
Admit for pertussis treatment with macrolide and apnoea monitoring.
Treat presumed bronchiolitis supportively and avoid contact prophylaxis review.
Give the next routine pertussis vaccine dose as the primary acute treatment.
explanations: Young infants with pertussis may be afebrile yet have life-threatening apnoea. Diagnostic samples can be collected promptly, but a suggestive exposure and paroxysmal cough with cyanosis require inpatient evaluation.
A macrolide can reduce transmission and may benefit early disease, but hypoxaemic apnoea episodes in a six-week-old warrant hospital monitoring regardless of fever or radiographic pneumonia.

Correct: a young partially immunised infant with coughing paroxysms, apnoea and household exposure has suspected pertussis. Admit for respiratory monitoring and supportive care, send PCR testing as appropriate, start an age-appropriate macrolide and give infection-control and contact prophylaxis advice.

Bronchiolitis can cause apnoea in small infants, but post-tussive cyanosis, a prolonged cough in a household contact and incomplete immunisation raise pertussis strongly. Isolation and exposure management should be considered.
Vaccination is crucial for future protection and contact strategies, but it is not treatment for an active infant illness. Provide macrolide and monitoring as clinically indicated.
pearl: Pertussis in young infants may cause apnoea rather than a characteristic whoop; protect high-risk household contacts.
pivot: An older immunised child with mild prolonged cough may receive outpatient evaluation depending on severity.

steps: Admit for pertussis treatment with macrolide and apnoea monitoring.
Nasopharyngeal PCR when indicated and macrolide per infant age/local dosing.
Droplet precautions and public-health notification/contact prophylaxis as indicated.
Feeding, hydration and family vaccination/cocooning advice.
management.safety: Do not prescribe unsafe cough suppressants or assume afebrile illness is benign.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

skill: Fat embolism syndrome after long-bone fracture
context: Advanced surgical and acute speciality decisions
stem: A 20-year-old two days after femoral fracture develops acute hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae across the upper chest. CXR shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates and platelet count has fallen. CT pulmonary angiography shows no major thrombus.
ask: Which diagnosis and management are MOST appropriate?
options: Support oxygenation and stabilise fractures in fat embolism syndrome.
Start full-dose anticoagulation for presumed occult thromboembolism.
Give IV antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia as the sole initial response.
Begin diuretics for presumed cardiogenic oedema after long-bone trauma.
Arrange routine systemic thrombolysis for suspected microscopic emboli.
explanations: Correct: respiratory and neurological involvement after long-bone trauma is typical; treatment is supportive. Clinical distinction: FES after long-bone fracture often presents 24–72 hours later with respiratory distress, confusion and petechiae.

Pulmonary embolism is a competing cause of hypoxaemia after trauma, but CTPA shows no major thrombus and the triad of hypoxaemia, neurological changes and petechiae after fracture is typical of fat embolism. Anticoagulation is not specific therapy for FES.

Aspiration or pneumonia can cause diffuse infiltrates and hypoxaemia but do not as readily account for petechiae, thrombocytopenia and neurological findings two days after a femoral fracture. Supportive critical care is the priority.
Fluid overload can contribute to hypoxaemia, but rash and altered mentation with the temporal fracture link support fat embolism; empiric diuresis may worsen haemodynamics without signs of overload.
Systemic thrombolysis targets major thrombotic emboli in selected unstable cases, not microscopic fat emboli. Bleeding risk is especially problematic in the recent-trauma setting.
pearl: FES after long-bone fracture often presents 24–72 hours later with respiratory distress, confusion and petechiae.
pivot: A haemodynamically unstable patient with new right ventricular strain may still need workup for thrombotic PE.

steps: Support oxygenation and stabilise fractures in fat embolism syndrome.
Exclude PE, infection and head injury; monitor ABG, neurological state and platelets.
Prompt fracture immobilisation/fixation when physiologically feasible.
Fluids balanced against ARDS, monitor kidneys and complications.
management.safety: Routine steroids and anticoagulation have no established role solely to treat FES.
management.local: Study summary only: obtain appropriate consultant and multidisciplinary guidance, verified drugs and local operative protocols.

stem: A 32-year-old presents with gum bleeding, bruising and fatigue. FBC shows Hb 82 g/L, platelets 22 ×10^9/L and abnormal promyelocytes on film. INR 1.7, fibrinogen 0.7 g/L, D-dimer high. Molecular confirmation is pending.
ask: Which intervention is MOST appropriate before molecular confirmation?
options: Give platelet transfusion as the only treatment until bone marrow confirmation.
Give ATRA immediately while treating coagulopathy in suspected APL.
Wait for PML–RARA molecular results before prescribing leukaemia therapy.
Start intensive induction chemotherapy first, adding ATRA only if confirmed.
Give IV heparin routinely to prevent the coagulopathy of acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
explanations: Blood products may be urgently required to correct thrombocytopenia and low fibrinogen, but they do not suppress the underlying promyelocytic leukaemia. ATRA must begin as soon as APL is strongly suspected.

Correct: suspected APL is a haematological emergency with early fatal DIC; ATRA should not wait for PML-RARA confirmation. Clinical distinction: APL is 'treat on suspicion': ATRA can rapidly reduce coagulopathy-driven early deaths.

Waiting for molecular confirmation may lead to catastrophic intracranial or other bleeding from APL-associated DIC. Start ATRA immediately while arranging definitive testing and haematology-directed supportive transfusions.

Definitive induction is specialist-directed and depends on risk and confirmation, but ATRA should not be postponed until chemotherapy starts. Early differentiation therapy is a unique lifesaving priority.
Heparin is not routine first-line treatment for APL coagulopathy in a bleeding-prone patient with low fibrinogen and platelets. Correct coagulopathy aggressively and start disease-directed therapy.
pearl: APL is 'treat on suspicion': ATRA can rapidly reduce coagulopathy-driven early deaths.
pivot: Other AML subtypes need prompt specialist treatment, but APL is uniquely time-critical for empiric ATRA.

steps: Give ATRA immediately while treating coagulopathy in suspected APL.
Start all-trans retinoic acid via haematology and send molecular testing.
Support platelets, fibrinogen and coagulation targets with blood products per APL pathway.
DIC, differentiation syndrome, organ function and infection.
management.safety: Avoid invasive procedures until coagulopathy is controlled.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

context: Advanced GP psychiatry ethics and safe prescribing
stem: A 47-year-old takes diazepam 25 mg daily for five years. His supply ended four days ago. He now has severe anxiety, tremor, insomnia, sweating and a generalised seizure. Glucose and electrolytes are normal.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give an SSRI now and taper diazepam rapidly without replacement dosing.
Treat the seizure once, then discharge with strict abstinence instructions.
Switch to a short-acting sedative and stop all benzodiazepines the next day.
Give antipsychotic monotherapy to control agitation and prevent further seizures.
Stabilise benzodiazepine withdrawal, then gradually taper under supervision.
explanations: An SSRI may treat an underlying anxiety disorder over time but cannot acutely prevent recurrent benzodiazepine withdrawal seizures. Safe withdrawal usually requires re-stabilisation with an appropriate benzodiazepine and planned taper.

Withdrawal seizures after long-term daily diazepam imply a medically significant withdrawal syndrome requiring observation and management. One acute seizure treatment without stabilisation leaves recurrence risk.

Rapid cessation after long-term benzodiazepine exposure can provoke further seizures and autonomic symptoms. Taper speed should be individualised after stabilising acute withdrawal, often over an extended period.
Antipsychotics do not correct the GABAergic withdrawal mechanism and can lower seizure threshold in some circumstances. They should not replace benzodiazepine-based withdrawal management.

Correct: a withdrawal seizure signals complicated high-risk dependence requiring monitored management. Clinical distinction: Abrupt benzodiazepine cessation can be dangerous after chronic use; slow taper and monitoring are safer.
pearl: Abrupt benzodiazepine cessation can be dangerous after chronic use; slow taper and monitoring are safer.
pivot: Brief low-dose use without dependence may produce rebound insomnia without severe withdrawal.

steps: Stabilise benzodiazepine withdrawal, then gradually taper under supervision.
Supervised benzodiazepine regimen, titrate then gradually taper based on dependence and risk.
Autonomic instability, seizures, delirium, mental state and sedation.
CBT for anxiety/insomnia, non-addictive treatments and coordinated prescriber follow-up.
